Matrices as transformations, for programmers

A matrix as a linear map (its columns are the images of the basis), the matrix-vector product by rows and by columns, the catalog of plane transformations, composition and its cost, the determinant as signed volume, rank, null space, inverse and condition number, affine transformations in homogeneous coordinates, and why a network without activations collapses into a single matrix. With a from-scratch module verified against NumPy, the calibration of a badly mounted accelerometer and a worked example by hand.

Summary

  • A linear map is pinned down by the images of the basis vectors: those images are the columns of its matrix. is the combination of columns with weights , or, by rows, dot products.
  • Rotations and reflections are orthogonal matrices (): they preserve norms, angles and dot products. Scalings, shears and projections do not.
  • Composing is multiplying, right to left: “first , then ” is . It is associative but not commutative, and the grouping order changes the cost from to .
  • is the signed volume factor. ⇔ rank-deficient ⇔ nontrivial null space ⇔ no inverse. What measures numerical sensitivity is the condition number , not the determinant.
  • To solve use np.linalg.solve (LU), never inv(A) @ b.
  • A layer is . Without , any number of layers is a single affine map.

§1 · Linear maps

The columns are the images of the basis

A map is linear if it respects sums and scaling:

Since every can be written in the standard basis, linearity gives : knowing the images is enough. Placed as columns they form the matrix , and . Immediate consequences: , lines go to lines (or to points) and parallel lines stay parallel.

The product can be computed in two equivalent ways:

By rows, each component is the dot product of a row with (topic 2): this is the “ linear models at once” reading. By columns, is a linear combination of the columns: this is the geometric reading, and it says that all possible outputs form the column space . With the matrix from the simple version:

Cost: multiplications. In code, with the data in a matrix with one observation per row (the NumPy, pandas and scikit-learn convention), transforming all rows at once is X @ A.T, not A @ X: . Forgetting the transpose is one of the most common bugs; with square matrices it raises no shape error, it just gives wrong results.

§2 · Catalog

Rotations, scalings, reflections, shears and projections

The five families of plane transformations that show up everywhere:

TransformationMatrixdetPreserves
rotation by angle θ1norms, angles, areas, orientation
scalingaxes; angles only if
reflection across the line at angle φ−1norms, angles, areas; reverses orientation
horizontal shear1areas, horizontal lines
projection onto the line of ()0the points on the line ()

Rotations and reflections are orthogonal: their columns are unit length and perpendicular to each other, that is, and . Everything they preserve follows from that:

Euclidean distances and cosine similarities (topics 1 and 2) are invariant under any orthogonal transformation: that is why PCA, which rotates the data into the basis of its components, does not change distances if all components are kept. An orthogonal projection is symmetric and idempotent (); projecting onto a -dimensional subspace with orthonormal basis is , and keeping the coordinates is , which is what PCA does when it reduces dimension.

An idea the widget shows and that will come back in upcoming topics: every matrix sends the unit circle to an ellipse. Its semi-axes are the singular values (the square roots of the eigenvalues of ), and . An orthogonal matrix has : the circle stays a circle.

A e₁ (column 1) A e₂ (column 2) image of the unit square (area = |det|) image of the unit circle (semi-axes σ₁, σ₂)

§3 · Composition

Multiplying is chaining, and order matters

If and then , then . The product is defined precisely so that this holds: its column is applied to column of , and its entry is the dot product of row of with column of :

It is read right to left: is “first , then ”. Properties:

  • Associative: . Chaining does not depend on how you group.
  • Not commutative: in general . With the 90° rotation and , and . Things that do commute include, for example, two plane rotations, or a uniform scaling with anything.
  • Transpose and inverse reverse the order: , (to undo “put on your socks, then your shoes” you have to take your shoes off first).
  • : volume factors multiply.

Cost. The product of two matrices costs multiplications with the direct algorithm (BLAS uses that same order with cache-optimized blocks; subcubic Strassen-type algorithms are rarely used in practice because of stability and constants). Matrix times vector costs . So, to apply a chain to a vector, group from the right:

If the same chain is applied to many vectors ( columns or rows of data), it pays to form once. For chains of rectangular matrices, the optimal order is chosen by dynamic programming (the classic matrix chain problem; np.linalg.multi_dot does it for you).

composicion.py · actual output (n = 2000; timings are from this machine)

import time, numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 2000
A, B = rng.normal(size=(n, n)), rng.normal(size=(n, n)); x = rng.normal(size=n)
print("associativity |(AB)x - A(Bx)| / |A(Bx)| =", f"{np.linalg.norm((A @ B) @ x - A @ (B @ x)) / np.linalg.norm(A @ (B @ x)):.1e}")
print("commutativity |AB - BA| / |AB| =", round(np.linalg.norm(A @ B - B @ A) / np.linalg.norm(A @ B), 3))
def t(f, k=3):
    best = 1e9
    for _ in range(k):
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); f(); best = min(best, time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return best
print(f"multiplications: (AB)x = n^3 + n^2 = {n**3 + n**2:.2e}   A(Bx) = 2 n^2 = {2 * n**2:.2e}")
print(f"time (AB)x {t(lambda: (A @ B) @ x) * 1e3:.1f} ms   A(Bx) {t(lambda: A @ (B @ x)) * 1e3:.2f} ms")

# associativity |(AB)x - A(Bx)| / |A(Bx)| = 1.4e-15
# commutativity |AB - BA| / |AB| = 1.414
# multiplications: (AB)x = n^3 + n^2 = 8.00e+09   A(Bx) = 2 n^2 = 8.00e+06

§4 · Determinant, rank and inverse

How much volume is stretched and when it can be undone

The determinant is the factor by which multiplies areas (in 2D) or volumes (in D), with a negative sign if it reverses orientation. For :

which is the signed area of the parallelogram formed by the two columns. Its properties follow from that reading: , , , and it is linear in each column and changes sign when two columns are swapped. To compute it you don’t use cofactor expansion () but Gaussian elimination with pivoting, , in :

with the number of row swaps (§7). For square , these are equivalent:

The rank is the dimension of the column space, and the null space is the set of directions that get flattened; . In the “flatten” matrix from the simple version, , the second column is twice the first: rank 1 and null space spanned by . Two points that differ by a multiple of go to the same place, and no inverse is possible. For , if it exists:

Don’t compute the inverse to solve systems. is solved by factoring (about operations) and doing forward and back substitution ( per right-hand side); inverting costs about and, above all, is less accurate: solve is backward stable (it exactly solves a very nearby system, with a residual on the order of machine epsilon), inv(A) @ b is not. If there are many right-hand sides, reuse the factorization (scipy.linalg.lu_factor / lu_solve).

Condition number. What measures how much amplifies errors is not the determinant but

The determinant depends on scale: has and , perfectly conditioned. Rule of thumb: with you lose about of the 16 digits of a float64. In ML it shows up in the normal equations of linear regression: , and nearly redundant columns make it blow up (§8 and the upcoming topic 4, least squares as a projection).

condicion.py · actual output

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n = 300
U, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(n, n))); V, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(n, n)))
s = np.logspace(0, -10, n)                       # singular values from 1 to 1e-10: kappa = 1e10
A = U @ np.diag(s) @ V.T
x_true = rng.normal(size=n); b = A @ x_true
print(f"kappa(A) = {np.linalg.cond(A):.2e}")
for nombre, x in [("solve(A, b)", np.linalg.solve(A, b)), ("inv(A) @ b", np.linalg.inv(A) @ b)]:
    print(f"{nombre:12s} relative residual {np.linalg.norm(A @ x - b) / np.linalg.norm(b):.1e}   relative error in x {np.linalg.norm(x - x_true) / np.linalg.norm(x_true):.1e}")
# amplification of an error in b (bound: kappa)
db = rng.normal(size=n); db *= 1e-8 * np.linalg.norm(b) / np.linalg.norm(db)
dx = np.linalg.solve(A, b + db) - np.linalg.solve(A, b)
print(f"relative error in b 1.0e-08 -> in x {np.linalg.norm(dx) / np.linalg.norm(x_true):.1e}")

# kappa(A) = 1.00e+10
# solve(A, b)  relative residual 1.1e-15   relative error in x 1.2e-07
# inv(A) @ b   relative residual 2.5e-07   relative error in x 2.1e-06
# relative error in b 1.0e-08 -> in x 2.8e+00

With , both methods lose about 10 digits in (that is the problem, not the algorithm), but solve leaves a residual on the order of and the inverse is eight orders of magnitude worse, with a larger error in too. The last line is the bound in action: a relative error of in produces one of almost 3 in , a factor of , below .

§5 · Affine maps and homogeneous coordinates

Translating is multiplying too (with one more dimension)

A translation is not linear (it moves the origin). An affine map is not either, but it becomes linear by adding a fixed coordinate equal to 1:

With these matrices, composing rotations, scalings and translations is a product again. It is the standard in graphics, computer vision and robotics (vehicle poses as matrices in or ). In the fleet: to rotate the plane around a depot instead of the origin, you translate to the origin, rotate and translate back, ; to convert GPS positions to a local frame with its origin at the depot and axes aligned with its street, the same. A network layer is exactly an affine map.

homogenea.py · actual output

import numpy as np
from matrices import homogenea, rotacion, matmul, matvec
# rotate 30° around the depot D = (3, 2) km: translate D to the origin, rotate, translate back
D = [3.0, 2.0]
T_menos = homogenea([[1, 0], [0, 1]], [-D[0], -D[1]])
R = homogenea(rotacion(30), [0, 0])
T_mas = homogenea([[1, 0], [0, 1]], D)
M = matmul(T_mas, matmul(R, T_menos))
print(np.round(M, 4))
p = [5.0, 2.0, 1.0]                       # customer 2 km east of the depot
print("customer rotated:", np.round(matvec(M, p), 4))
print("the depot does not move:", np.round(matvec(M, [3.0, 2.0, 1.0]), 4))

# [[ 0.866  -0.5     1.4019]
#  [ 0.5     0.866  -1.2321]
#  [ 0.      0.      1.    ]]
# customer rotated: [4.7321 3.     1.    ]
# the depot does not move: [3. 2. 1.]

§6 · Network layers

σ(Wx + b), and why without σ there is no network

A dense layer computes , with (each row is a neuron: a dot product with the input, topic 2), and applied elementwise, for example . Without , stacking layers adds nothing:

Moreover, the rank of is limited by the narrowest layer: a linear network with a “bottleneck” of width can only represent maps of rank (and its optimum under squared loss is the PCA solution; Baldi and Hornik, 1989). Nonlinearity is what gives expressiveness: a network with one sufficiently wide hidden layer approximates any continuous function on a compact set (Cybenko, 1989; Hornik, 1991). With ReLU, the network is piecewise linear: each neuron folds the space along the hyperplane .

The layer from the simple version separates trucks whose engine-oil temperature difference is anomalous on either side. With and :

so the linear rule in the hidden space is in the original one: two half-planes, a boundary no straight line can give. Here has rank 1 on purpose: only matters.

capas.py · actual output

import json, numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
# three layers without activation = a single affine layer
W = [rng.normal(size=(8, 4)), rng.normal(size=(6, 8)), rng.normal(size=(2, 6))]
b = [rng.normal(size=8), rng.normal(size=6), rng.normal(size=2)]
X = rng.normal(size=(1000, 4))
H = X
for Wi, bi in zip(W, b):
    H = H @ Wi.T + bi
Wt = W[2] @ W[1] @ W[0]; bt = W[2] @ (W[1] @ b[0] + b[1]) + b[2]
print("no activation: |net - (W x + b)| max =", f"{np.abs(H - (X @ Wt.T + bt)).max():.1e}", " total W", Wt.shape)
H = X
for Wi, bi in zip(W, b):
    H = np.maximum(0, H @ Wi.T + bi)
print("with ReLU:     |net - (W x + b)| max =", f"{np.abs(H - (X @ Wt.T + bt)).max():.2f}")
# the layer from the simple version (engine and oil temperatures)
d = json.load(open("../embed.json")); X = np.array(d["X"]); y = np.array(d["y"])
W1 = np.array([[1.0, -1.0], [-1.0, 1.0]]); b1 = np.array([-0.8, -0.8])
H = np.maximum(0, X @ W1.T + b1)
print("ReLU layer + rule h1 + h2 > 0: errors", int(((H.sum(1) > 0) != y).sum()), "of", len(y))
mejor = len(y)                                   # the best possible line: exhaustive search
for th in np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 1441)[:-1]:
    u = np.sort(X @ [np.cos(th), np.sin(th)]); cortes = np.r_[u[0] - 1, (u[1:] + u[:-1]) / 2]
    mejor = min(mejor, min(int(((X @ [np.cos(th), np.sin(th)] > t) != y).sum()) for t in cortes))
print("best line on the original data: errors", mejor, "of", len(y))

# no activation: |net - (W x + b)| max = 1.6e-14  total W (2, 4)
# with ReLU:     |net - (W x + b)| max = 23.93
# ReLU layer + rule h1 + h2 > 0: errors 0 of 160
# best line on the original data: errors 23 of 160

§7 · From scratch

Product, determinant, systems and inverse, verified

Python lists of lists, no NumPy in the computations. The central piece is LU factorization with partial pivoting: in each column the entry with the largest absolute value is chosen as the pivot, which bounds the multipliers by 1 and avoids dividing by small numbers (without pivoting, gives floating-point garbage).

matrices.py

"""Matrices as transformations, from scratch (lists of lists, no NumPy in the computations)."""


def forma(A):
    return len(A), len(A[0])


def matvec(A, x):
    """A x by rows: each component is the dot product of a row of A with x."""
    if len(A[0]) != len(x):
        raise ValueError("columns of A != length of x")
    return [sum(a * b for a, b in zip(fila, x)) for fila in A]


def matvec_columnas(A, x):
    """A x by columns: x1 * (column 1) + x2 * (column 2) + ..."""
    m, n = forma(A)
    y = [0.0] * m
    for j in range(n):
        for i in range(m):
            y[i] += x[j] * A[i][j]
    return y


def matmul(A, B):
    """(AB)_ij = row i of A · column j of B.  Cost: m*n*p multiplications."""
    m, n = forma(A)
    n2, p = forma(B)
    if n != n2:
        raise ValueError("incompatible dimensions")
    Bt = list(zip(*B))
    return [[sum(a * b for a, b in zip(fila, col)) for col in Bt] for fila in A]


def identidad(n):
    return [[1.0 if i == j else 0.0 for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]


def lu(A):
    """Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting: P A = L U.
    Returns (LU packed into one matrix, permutation, number of swaps)."""
    n = len(A)
    M = [list(map(float, fila)) for fila in A]
    perm = list(range(n))
    cambios = 0
    for k in range(n):
        p = max(range(k, n), key=lambda i: abs(M[i][k]))     # pivot: the largest in absolute value
        if M[p][k] == 0.0:
            raise ZeroDivisionError("singular matrix")
        if p != k:
            M[k], M[p] = M[p], M[k]
            perm[k], perm[p] = perm[p], perm[k]
            cambios += 1
        for i in range(k + 1, n):
            f = M[i][k] / M[k][k]
            M[i][k] = f                                       # store the multiplier (L part)
            for j in range(k + 1, n):
                M[i][j] -= f * M[k][j]
    return M, perm, cambios


def det(A):
    """Determinant = product of the pivots, with sign (-1)^swaps. 0 if singular."""
    try:
        M, _, c = lu(A)
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        return 0.0
    d = -1.0 if c % 2 else 1.0
    for k in range(len(A)):
        d *= M[k][k]
    return d


def solve(A, b):
    """Solves A x = b with LU: forward (L) and back (U) substitution. Without computing the inverse."""
    M, perm, _ = lu(A)
    n = len(A)
    y = [float(b[perm[i]]) for i in range(n)]
    for i in range(n):                       # L y = P b  (L with ones on the diagonal)
        y[i] -= sum(M[i][j] * y[j] for j in range(i))
    x = [0.0] * n
    for i in reversed(range(n)):             # U x = y
        x[i] = (y[i] - sum(M[i][j] * x[j] for j in range(i + 1, n))) / M[i][i]
    return x


def inversa(A):
    """Inverse by solving A X = I column by column (a single LU factorization)."""
    n = len(A)
    M, perm, _ = lu(A)
    cols = []
    for k in range(n):
        e = [1.0 if perm[i] == k else 0.0 for i in range(n)]
        for i in range(n):
            e[i] -= sum(M[i][j] * e[j] for j in range(i))
        x = [0.0] * n
        for i in reversed(range(n)):
            x[i] = (e[i] - sum(M[i][j] * x[j] for j in range(i + 1, n))) / M[i][i]
        cols.append(x)
    return [list(f) for f in zip(*cols)]


def traspuesta(A):
    return [list(c) for c in zip(*A)]


def rotacion(grados):
    import math
    t = math.radians(grados)
    return [[math.cos(t), -math.sin(t)], [math.sin(t), math.cos(t)]]


def homogenea(A, t):
    """(n+1)x(n+1) matrix that applies x -> A x + t in homogeneous coordinates."""
    n = len(A)
    return [list(A[i]) + [t[i]] for i in range(n)] + [[0.0] * n + [1.0]]

check.py · 300 random problems (dimensions 2 to 8) · actual output

import numpy as np
from matrices import matvec, matvec_columnas, matmul, det, solve, inversa, homogenea, rotacion

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
e = dict(mv=0, mvc=0, mm=0, det=0, solve=0, inv=0, res=0)
for _ in range(300):
    n = int(rng.integers(2, 9)); m = int(rng.integers(2, 9)); p = int(rng.integers(2, 9))
    A = rng.normal(size=(m, n)); B = rng.normal(size=(n, p)); x = rng.normal(size=n)
    S = rng.normal(size=(n, n)); b = rng.normal(size=n)
    rel = lambda u, v: np.max(np.abs(np.array(u) - v)) / np.max(np.abs(v))
    e["mv"] = max(e["mv"], rel(matvec(A.tolist(), x.tolist()), A @ x))
    e["mvc"] = max(e["mvc"], rel(matvec_columnas(A.tolist(), x.tolist()), A @ x))
    e["mm"] = max(e["mm"], rel(matmul(A.tolist(), B.tolist()), A @ B))
    e["det"] = max(e["det"], abs(det(S.tolist()) - np.linalg.det(S)) / abs(np.linalg.det(S)))
    xs = solve(S.tolist(), b.tolist())
    e["solve"] = max(e["solve"], rel(xs, np.linalg.solve(S, b)))
    e["res"] = max(e["res"], np.max(np.abs(S @ xs - b)))
    e["inv"] = max(e["inv"], rel(inversa(S.tolist()), np.linalg.inv(S)))
print(f"matvec (by rows) vs A @ x              {e['mv']:.1e}")
print(f"matvec_columnas vs A @ x               {e['mvc']:.1e}")
print(f"matmul vs A @ B                        {e['mm']:.1e}")
print(f"det vs np.linalg.det (relative)        {e['det']:.1e}")
print(f"solve vs np.linalg.solve (relative)    {e['solve']:.1e}")
print(f"max residual |S x - b|                 {e['res']:.1e}")
print(f"inversa vs np.linalg.inv (relative)    {e['inv']:.1e}")
print("det of a singular matrix (row 2 = 2 x row 1):", det([[1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6], [1, 0, 1]]))
H = homogenea(rotacion(30), [5, -2]); x = [1.0, 2.0, 1.0]
R = np.array(rotacion(30)); print(f"homogenea vs R x + t                   {np.max(np.abs(np.array(matvec(H, x))[:2] - (R @ [1, 2] + [5, -2]))):.1e}")

# matvec (by rows) vs A @ x              5.2e-16
# matvec_columnas vs A @ x               4.4e-16
# matmul vs A @ B                        3.3e-16
# det vs np.linalg.det (relative)        3.0e-14
# solve vs np.linalg.solve (relative)    3.0e-14
# max residual |S x - b|                 6.6e-14
# inversa vs np.linalg.inv (relative)    3.1e-14
# det of a singular matrix (row 2 = 2 x row 1): 0.0
# homogenea vs R x + t                   1.7e-16

The differences are on the order of machine epsilon () times the condition number of each random problem; the product, which does not divide, stays at . For the singular matrix, elimination finds a pivot that is exactly 0 and det returns 0 instead of a tiny number: NumPy, which does not stop, would return something on the order of , which should also be read as zero.

§8 · In the fleet

A badly mounted accelerometer and two columns that are one

Sensor orientation. The telemetry box measures accelerations in its own axes, and it is almost never aligned with the truck. If is the rotation from the box axes to the truck axes, . It is estimated from two references: with the truck stopped, the accelerometer only sees gravity, which gives the “up” axis ; on straight stretches, the horizontal part of the reading should follow the acceleration given by the derivative of the GPS speed, and the direction that best follows it by least squares is “forward” . With , the rows of are , an orthogonal matrix by construction. We simulate 10 minutes at 10 Hz with the box rotated 60° in yaw, 4° in pitch and −6° in roll.

flota.py

import numpy as np
from matrices import rotacion
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True)

# ---- 1. A 10-minute trip at 10 Hz in truck axes: x forward, y left, z up
hz, T = 10, 600; t = np.arange(T * hz) / hz
a_lon = np.zeros_like(t)                                    # longitudinal acceleration (m/s²)
for t0, dur, a in [(5, 20, 0.9), (60, 8, -1.5), (90, 15, 0.8), (200, 4, -4.0), (215, 18, 0.7),
                   (330, 10, -1.2), (400, 22, 0.6), (520, 3, -3.2), (560, 6.2 / 1.3, -1.3)]:
    a_lon[(t >= t0) & (t < t0 + dur)] = a
v = np.clip(np.cumsum(a_lon) / hz, 0, None)                 # speed (m/s): starts and ends stopped
w = 0.06 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 75) * (v > 3)             # turn rate (rad/s) on gentle curves
a_veh = np.c_[a_lon, v * w, np.full_like(t, 9.81)]          # the accelerometer also measures gravity

# ---- 2. The box is mounted rotated: yaw 60°, pitch 4°, roll -6°
def Rz(g): return np.array([[np.cos(g), -np.sin(g), 0], [np.sin(g), np.cos(g), 0], [0, 0, 1]])
def Ry(g): return np.array([[np.cos(g), 0, np.sin(g)], [0, 1, 0], [-np.sin(g), 0, np.cos(g)]])
def Rx(g): return np.array([[1, 0, 0], [0, np.cos(g), -np.sin(g)], [0, np.sin(g), np.cos(g)]])
R_true = Rz(np.radians(60)) @ Ry(np.radians(4)) @ Rx(np.radians(-6))     # box -> truck
a_dev = a_veh @ R_true + rng.normal(0, 0.15, (len(t), 3))               # = (R_trueᵀ a_veh)ᵀ by rows + noise

# ---- 3. Estimate the orientation from two signals: gravity and the GPS acceleration
parado = v < 0.1                                            # according to the GPS
z = a_dev[parado].mean(0); z /= np.linalg.norm(z)           # "up" in box axes: gravity only
h = a_dev - np.outer(a_dev @ z, z)                          # horizontal part (remove gravity)
a_gps = np.gradient(v, 1 / hz) + rng.normal(0, 0.1, len(t)) # derivative of the GPS speed
recto = np.abs(w + rng.normal(0, 0.002, len(t))) < 0.01   # straight stretches according to the GPS heading
x = h[recto].T @ a_gps[recto]                               # "forward" direction: the one that best follows a_gps
x -= (x @ z) * z; x /= np.linalg.norm(x)
y = np.cross(z, x)
R_est = np.vstack([x, y, z])                                # rows = truck axes seen from the box
a_rot = a_dev @ R_est.T

print("R_est R_estᵀ - I, max:", f"{np.abs(R_est @ R_est.T - np.eye(3)).max():.1e}", "  det:", round(np.linalg.det(R_est), 6))
ang = np.degrees(np.arccos((np.trace(R_est @ R_true.T) - 1) / 2))
print(f"orientation error: {ang:.2f}°")
print("stopped, box axes:", a_dev[parado].mean(0), "  truck axes:", a_rot[parado].mean(0), f"  ({parado.sum()} samples)")
k = (t >= 200) & (t < 204)                                  # the hard braking
print("hard braking, box axes  :", a_dev[k].mean(0))
print("hard braking, truck axes:", a_rot[k].mean(0), " true:", a_veh[k].mean(0))
print("RMSE per axis vs the truth (m/s²):", np.sqrt(np.mean((a_rot - a_veh)**2, 0)), "  uncorrected:", np.sqrt(np.mean((a_dev - a_veh)**2, 0)))
suave = lambda a: np.convolve(a, np.ones(hz) / hz, "same")  # 1 s moving average
eventos = lambda m: int(np.sum(np.diff(m.astype(int)) == 1))
for nombre, A in [("box", a_dev), ("corrected", a_rot), ("true", a_veh)]:
    print(f"{nombre:9s}: hard brakes (forward < -2.5) {eventos(suave(A[:, 0]) < -2.5)}   sharp turns (|lateral| > 2) {eventos(np.abs(suave(A[:, 1])) > 2)}")

# ---- 4. Redundant columns: km and miles in the same regression
n = 400
km = rng.uniform(20, 400, n); paradas = rng.integers(0, 15, n)
litros = 0.31 * km + 2.0 * paradas + rng.normal(0, 4, n)
millas = np.round(km * 0.621371, 1)                         # the same distance, rounded to 0.1
X2 = np.c_[np.ones(n), km, paradas]; X3 = np.c_[X2, millas]
print(f"\ncond(X) without miles {np.linalg.cond(X2):.1e}   with miles {np.linalg.cond(X3):.1e}")
co = []
for r in range(5):
    i = rng.integers(0, n, n)                               # bootstrap resampling
    b3 = np.linalg.lstsq(X3[i], litros[i], rcond=None)[0]; b2 = np.linalg.lstsq(X2[i], litros[i], rcond=None)[0]
    co.append(b3); print(f"  sample {r}: with miles km={b3[1]:+8.3f} miles={b3[3]:+8.3f} (km + 0.621·miles = {b3[1] + 0.621371 * b3[3]:.3f})   without miles km={b2[1]:.3f}")
xq = np.array([1, 250, 6, round(250 * 0.621371, 1)])
print("prediction for 250 km and 6 stops across the 5 samples:", np.round([xq @ c for c in co], 2))

actual output

# stopped, box axes: [-0.696 -1.02   9.733]   truck axes: [ 0.    -0.     9.811]   (405 samples)
# hard braking, box axes  : [-3.162  2.169  9.901]
# hard braking, truck axes: [-3.997 -0.547  9.821]  true: [-4.    -0.528  9.81 ]
# RMSE per axis vs the truth (m/s²): [0.15 0.15 0.15]   uncorrected: [0.854 1.194 0.18 ]
# box      : hard brakes (forward < -2.5) 2   sharp turns (|lateral| > 2) 1
# corrected: hard brakes (forward < -2.5) 2   sharp turns (|lateral| > 2) 0
# true     : hard brakes (forward < -2.5) 2   sharp turns (|lateral| > 2) 0

# cond(X) without miles 6.9e+02   with miles 1.2e+04
#   sample 0: with miles km=  -7.580 miles= +12.702 (km + 0.621·miles = 0.313)   without miles km=0.313
#   sample 1: with miles km=  +2.123 miles=  -2.913 (km + 0.621·miles = 0.313)   without miles km=0.313
#   sample 2: with miles km=  -1.316 miles=  +2.614 (km + 0.621·miles = 0.309)   without miles km=0.309
#   sample 3: with miles km=  +0.678 miles=  -0.596 (km + 0.621·miles = 0.308)   without miles km=0.308
#   sample 4: with miles km=  +0.939 miles=  -1.004 (km + 0.621·miles = 0.315)   without miles km=0.315
# prediction for 250 km and 6 stops across the 5 samples: [89.05 89.27 89.46 89.45 89.44]

The estimated orientation is within 0.07° of the true one and is orthogonal up to rounding. With the truck stopped, the box “sees” −0.70 and −1.02 m/s² on its x and y axes: that is gravity leaking in through the tilt of the mounting, and an event detector would take it for real acceleration. During the −4 m/s² braking, the box reads −3.16 “forward” and +2.17 sideways: enough to trigger a sharp turn alert that never happened. After the rotation, the braking shows up entirely on the longitudinal axis (−4.00) and the per-axis errors drop to the sensor noise level (0.15 m/s²). In production the estimate is repeated periodically (the box moves) and more stretches and robust filters are used, but the math is this.

Redundant columns. In the second part, the trips table has the distance in kilometers and also in miles (rounded to 0.1). The design matrix becomes nearly singular: goes from about 700 to about 12,000. The km and miles coefficients change sign and size with every resample (from −7.6 to +2.1), because the null space of is almost the direction : any split with the same sum fits equally well. The predictions barely change, but interpreting or comparing those coefficients makes no sense. The fix: detect it in the exploratory analysis (correlations, , variance inflation factors) and drop one of the two, or regularize (ridge: has as its smallest eigenvalue).

§9 · Checklist

Before putting a matrix into a pipeline

  • A clear convention: column vectors () or one observation per row (X @ A.T)? Documented, and with a test using a non-symmetric matrix.
  • Composition order written right to left (“first B, then A” = ) and checked with a known point.
  • Chains applied to a vector grouped from the right; with many matrices, np.linalg.multi_dot.
  • Rotations: check and (a −1 is a reflection: swapped axes or a flipped sign).
  • Systems with solve or lstsq, never with inv; factor once if there are many right-hand sides.
  • Condition number measured; if is large, look for redundant columns, scale (topic 7 of Preparing the data) or regularize. Don’t use as a measure of singularity.
  • Units and axes of each sensor documented (east/north, latitude/longitude, box axes); orientation calibration repeated whenever the box can move.
  • In networks: check that there is an activation between linear layers (two Linear in a row with nothing in between are just one).

§10 · Worked example

One matrix, two orders and a system of liters and tolls

Matrix-vector product by rows and by columns, composition in both orders, determinant, inverse and two 2 × 2 fleet systems (one well conditioned and one not), by hand and with the numbers from the simple version.

The situation. The data team wants to infer how many hours a truck drove in the city and on the highway without having that data: they only know the diesel consumed and the toll paid. First, they review with the matrix from the simple version what it means to apply, chain and undo a transformation.

Example map

The matrix from idea 1 of the simple version, the rotation and the stretch from idea 3, and the liters-and-tolls matrix. We work out by hand where a point ends up, what happens when chaining in both orders, how much the area changes, how to undo it, and how to recover a truck’s hours from its liters and its toll. At the end, why swapping the toll for CO₂ ruins everything.

  1. Where the point (3, 2) ends up.
  2. Rotating and stretching, in both orders.
  3. The area factor.
  4. Undoing: the inverse.
  5. From liters and toll to hours.
  6. Liters and CO₂: an ill-conditioned system.

  1. Where the point (3, 2) ends up

    In words

    The matrix sends the → arrow to (2, 1) and the ↑ arrow to (−1, 1): those are its columns. The point (3, 2) is “3 steps → and 2 steps ↑”, so it ends up at 3 times the first column plus 2 times the second.

    The math, by columns

    The same math, by rows

    Why do they come out the same?

    Both ways add up the same four products , just grouped differently: by columns you add whole vectors first; by rows, each component separately (a dot product, topic 2). No constant comes from outside: they are the numbers from the toy in idea 1.

    What it means: the point (3, 2) ends up at (4, 5). The transformed grid takes each crossing (i, j) to the point : that is why knowing the columns is enough.

  2. Rotating and stretching, in both orders

    In words

    rotates 90° counterclockwise: it sends → to ↑ and ↑ to ←. stretches × 2 sideways. “First rotate, then stretch” is the matrix (the second step’s matrix goes on the left).

    The math

    Where does each entry come from?

    The entry (row , column ) of is the dot product of row of with column of . Check with the point: and stretching gives ; in the other order, and rotating gives .

    What it means: the same point ends up in different places depending on the order. It is the truck from idea 3: rotated and then stretched, it ends up “fat”; stretched and then rotated, it ends up “tall”.

  3. The area factor

    In words

    The square with side 1 turns into the parallelogram with sides (2, 1) and (−1, 1). Its signed area is the determinant.

    The math

    Why ?

    Fit the parallelogram inside the rectangle with sides and (here, 3 by 2) and subtract the corner triangles and rectangles: what remains is . The sign is positive because column 2 is rotated counterclockwise from column 1, like ↑ from →.

    What it means: multiplies every area by 3 and flips nothing over. Rotating does not change areas and stretching doubles them, so the chain doubles them, in either order.

  4. Undoing: the inverse

    In words

    Since the determinant is not 0, the transformation can be undone. The inverse of a 2 × 2 is obtained by swapping the diagonal, flipping the sign of the other two numbers and dividing by the determinant.

    The math

    Where does the 1/3 come from?

    It is : if multiplies areas by 3, undoing it has to divide them by 3 (). If the determinant were 0, you would have to divide by 0: that is why a matrix that flattens has no inverse.

    What it means: from (4, 5) you get back exactly to (3, 2). In code you don’t compute : you solve with solve, which does this same elimination without forming the inverse.

  5. From liters and toll to hours

    In words

    A truck used 92 liters and paid $18 in tolls. How many hours did it drive in the city () and on the highway ()? It means undoing the cost matrix from idea 1.

    The math

    What is each number?

    14liters of diesel per hour in the city
    25liters per hour on the highway
    0dollars of toll per hour in the city
    9dollars of toll per hour on the highway
    92, 18what was measured: liters (refueling) and dollars (toll card)

    These are the example values from idea 1 of the simple version, not real rates. The matrix is triangular (a 0 in the bottom left), so it is solved from the bottom up: it is the back substitution of §7.

    What it means: 3 hours in the city and 2 on the highway. If the liters were 93 instead of 92 (a one-liter error), you would get : a 4-minute difference. The system is well conditioned ().

  6. Liters and CO₂: an ill-conditioned system

    In words

    Suppose that, instead of the toll, we have the kilograms of CO₂ computed by the telemetry. It looks like another piece of data, but the CO₂ comes from burning the same diesel: it is almost proportional to the liters. The second row is almost the first one multiplied by a number.

    The math

    Where do the 37, the 66.5 and the 244 come from?

    Burning one liter of diesel emits about 2.64 kg of CO₂: 14 L/h × 2.64 ≈ 37 kg/h in the city. On the highway the system uses a slightly different factor, 2.66 (25 × 2.66 = 66.5), and that small difference is the only thing that tells the two rows apart. 244 = 3 · 37 + 2 · 66.5 is the CO₂ of the same trip. For and we use Cramer’s rule: replace one column of the matrix with the data and divide by the determinant.

    How much the error was amplified

    What it means: a one-liter error (0.4%) turns “3 h in the city and 2 on the highway” into “14 h in the city and −4 on the highway”, which is nonsense. The determinant 6 looks like a normal number, but it is tiny compared to the products it subtracts (931 and 925): what warns you is the condition number, 1,102. With liters and CO₂ you don’t have two pieces of data, you have one and a half.

ejemplo.py · reproduces the numbers above

import numpy as np
from matrices import matvec, matvec_columnas, matmul, det, inversa, solve
A, p = [[2, -1], [1, 1]], [3, 2]
print("1.", matvec(A, p), matvec_columnas(A, p))
E, R = [[2, 0], [0, 1]], [[0, -1], [1, 0]]
print("2.", matmul(E, R), matmul(R, E), matvec(matmul(E, R), p), matvec(matmul(R, E), p))
print("3.", det(A), det(E), det(R), det(matmul(E, R)))
Ai = inversa(A); print("4.", np.round(Ai, 4).tolist(), matvec(Ai, [4, 5]), np.round(matmul(A, Ai), 12).tolist())
G, b = [[14, 25], [0, 9]], [92, 18]
print("5.", det(G), solve(G, b), np.round(inversa(G), 5).tolist())
G2, b2 = [[14, 25], [37, 66.5]], [92, 244]
print("6.", det(G2), np.round(solve(G2, b2), 6), np.round(solve(G2, [93, 244]), 3), f"cond = {np.linalg.cond(G2):.0f}", f"cond(G) = {np.linalg.cond(G):.2f}")

# 1. [4, 5] [4.0, 5.0]
# 2. [[0, -2], [1, 0]] [[0, -1], [2, 0]] [-4, 3] [-2, 6]
# 3. 3.0 2.0 1.0 2.0
# 4. [[0.3333, 0.3333], [-0.3333, 0.6667]] [3.0, 1.9999999999999998] [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]]
# 5. 126.0 [3.0, 2.0] [[0.07143, -0.19841], [0.0, 0.11111]]
# 6. 6.000000000000103 [3. 2.] [14.083 -4.167] cond = 1102 cond(G) = 7.02

What would change in a real system

  • More road types than measurements: with city, rural road and highway and only two data points (liters and toll) the system is , has infinitely many solutions, and needs extra information or constrained least squares.
  • More measurements than unknowns: many trips of the same truck give an overdetermined, noisy system; it is solved by least squares (topic 4).
  • Learned coefficients: the 14 L/h or the $9/h would come from a regression on historical data, with their uncertainty.
  • Watch the conditioning: adding a measurement almost proportional to another one (CO₂ and liters) adds no information and makes the system worse.
